rto2-what-rent-to-own-actually-is-and-th.reason: Answer (the store has no lever, so only honor keeps the account; and honest math means the total cost shown while shopping) sits in sections three and seven; ends on a warning about haste, not the answer.
rto2-what-rent-to-own-actually-is-and-th.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can a store keep a customer without holding them? In rent-to-own it has to. The customer can return the item any time and owe nothing, so the store has no lever. The only thing that holds an account is the customer choosing, again, to keep it. That makes honor the business. And honest math means putting the true total cost where the buyer can see it.
rto2-what-rent-to-own-actually-is-and-th.example: THE MEASURE ON THE LABEL. Say a television sells for $500 at a retail store. The FTC finding this lesson carries puts rent-to-own prices at two to three times retail, sometimes more, so the total to own that set this way could run $1,000 to $1,500 or more. A just weight puts that total on the label the shopper reads while shopping, beside the $500, so the customer chooses knowing. Nothing is hidden, and the renewal they keep paying is one they chose with open eyes.
rto2-what-rent-to-own-actually-is-and-th.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can a store keep a customer without holding them? Yes, and in this model it is the only way. With no balance to threaten and three agreements in four ending in a return, the store lives on renewals earned each week from a person free to stop. Honor holds the account. Honor also governs the price: a just weight, the total cost shown where the buyer can see it. Run the operation with excellence, weigh the price on Yahweh's scale, and the customer who stays has a reason to.

teen.open: Can a store keep you as a customer without trapping you? In rent-to-own it must. You can return the item any time and owe nothing, so only honor keeps you.
teen.close: So the store keeps customers by earning them every week, not by holding them. And honest math means showing the full cost up front, because Yahweh delights in a just weight.

senior.open: The title asks whether a store can keep a customer without holding them. In rent-to-own it must, because the customer may return the item at any time and owe nothing. The store has no lever; only honor keeps the account.
senior.close: So the answer is yes, by honor alone. The renewal is earned every week from someone free to stop. And the honest math the title promises is the just weight: the true total cost set where the shopper can read it before choosing.

rto3-inventory-control-on-rent-versus-si.reason: Builds through accounting buckets and depreciation; the plain answer (yes, idle units quietly cost floor space, capital and a write-down) is stated in section four, and the Word's verdict follows later.
rto3-inventory-control-on-rent-versus-si.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is your back room quietly losing money? If units are sitting there, yes. A unit held for rent earns nothing while it takes up floor space and capital, and if it sits long enough it gets written down. Nobody calls to tell you; it is a loss that happens by nothing happening. The Word calls the cure diligence: know the state of your flocks.
rto3-inventory-control-on-rent-versus-si.example: TWO RETURNS, TWO PATHS. Say two identical units come back to the store in the same week. One is cleaned, tested, repaired and made presentable that week, and by Saturday it is on rent again, earning. The other is set in the back to deal with later. Weeks pass, then months. Under the method those filings describe, once it is 270 days old and has sat 180 days in a row, it stops waiting as an asset and starts being written down. Same unit, same week back; one choice made the difference.
rto3-inventory-control-on-rent-versus-si.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is your back room quietly losing money? It is whenever goods sit unworked. The books themselves split every unit into on rent or held for rent, so you can see what is working and what is standing still. The Word names the idle choice plainly: the slothful man is brother to the waster (Proverbs 18:9), and the buried talent was taken (Matthew 25:29). Know your counts today, turn each return this week, and the back room becomes your supply line instead of your loss.

teen.open: Can a back room full of stuff lose money? Yes. Every item just sitting there earns nothing, and the longer it sits the more it gets written off.
teen.close: So idle stock is a quiet loss. The fix is simple: know what you have, fix returns fast, and get them working again. The Word says doing nothing is close kin to wasting.

senior.open: The title asks whether a back room can quietly lose money. It can. A unit held for rent earns nothing, occupies space and capital, and after enough idle months is written down, all without any event to announce it.
senior.close: So the answer is yes, and the remedy is diligence. Know how many units are on rent and how many sit, turn each return quickly, and remember Proverbs 18:9 and Matthew 25: the man who buried what he held lost it. Employed things multiply.

rto1-the-seat-you-are-in-and-every-seat-.reason: The title's claim (the current seat trains you, since faithfulness in least is faithfulness in much) is made in sections three and four, after the teacher's story; the lesson ends on the course's closing standard instead.
rto1-the-seat-you-are-in-and-every-seat-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How does the chair you sit in now train you for the corner office? Your character does not change when your title does. Whoever is faithful in the least is faithful in much (Luke 16:10). The general manager's integrity is the account manager's integrity, promoted. So the small seat is not a detour on the way up. It is the qualification.
rto1-the-seat-you-are-in-and-every-seat-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How is your current chair training you for the corner office? By testing the same faithfulness the bigger chair will need. The master in the parable made the servant ruler over many things only after he was faithful over a few (Matthew 25:21). Work your seat heartily, as to the Lord and not to men (Colossians 3:23), whoever is watching. The diligent man stands before kings (Proverbs 22:29). Every season teaches something, and the standard never drops because the seat is small.

teen.open: Does the job you have now matter for the job you want later? Yes. Being faithful in small things is how you prove you can be trusted with big ones.
teen.close: So your current seat is your training. Work it well, even when nobody is watching, because the person you are in the small job is the person you will be in the big one.

senior.open: The title claims your present chair trains you for the corner office. The lesson grounds it in Luke 16:10: faithfulness in the least is faithfulness in much, and a man's integrity is the same whatever his title.
senior.close: So the present seat is the proving ground. Faithful over a few things first, then over many (Matthew 25:21). Work every season heartily, as to the Lord, and the higher seat finds a person already qualified for it.

rto4-sales-the-delivery-is-the-close-the.reason: First paragraph states it plainly (three in four return, so the signature is the start and the renewal is the sale) and the last line lands it: sell what they will still be glad they took in week thirty.

rto5-collections-as-honor-not-pressure.reason: Opens with the answer (collections cannot be ugly here; the priority is to re-sell and educate, not squeeze) and ends on the operating rule: make keeping it possible, or part honourably and leave the door open.

rto6-customer-service-white-glove-in-som.reason: Opens on the setting (service in somebody's living room); the answer (honour all men, shown in actions not words) builds across the verses, and the ending lands the friction rule rather than the title's question.
rto6-customer-service-white-glove-in-som.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Would your customer feel honoured in their own living room? Only if you honour them in actions, not words. Yahweh asks you to honour all men (1 Peter 2:17), not only the pleasant ones or the ones whose account is current. In a home that means holding doors, looking on their things, keeping your word, and serving the same whether anyone is watching or not.
rto6-customer-service-white-glove-in-som.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Would your customer feel honoured in their own living room? They will when honour is something you do. Treat their floor, their doorway and their evening as the subject (Philippians 2:4). Do to them as you would want done to you (Luke 6:31). Serve as to the Lord, not for the manager's eye (Ephesians 6:6-7). Withhold no good that is in your power to give (Proverbs 3:27). Keep honour in the room, and that family will know they were respected.

teen.open: Would a customer feel respected when you come into their home? Only if you show it in what you do: holding doors, taking care of their space, keeping your word.
teen.close: So honour is an action. Treat people the way you would want to be treated, even when nobody is checking, and they will feel it in their own home.

senior.open: The title asks whether a customer would feel honoured in their own living room. The Word's answer is to honour all men (1 Peter 2:17), and the lesson insists that honour is shown in actions, not only spoken.
senior.close: So the answer rests on deeds. Do unto them as you would have done to you, serve as to the Lord rather than for the eye of a supervisor, and withhold no good it is in your hand to give. Then honour is not claimed; it is felt.

rto7-covenant-over-contract.reason: Opens on what a contract is for; the answer (a contract is the floor, covenant posture is the ceiling) arrives in section three and the three changes later; ends on the limit, not the answer.
rto7-covenant-over-contract.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why should a business promise aim higher than the paperwork? Because a contract is built for the day somebody walks away. It is the floor, not the ceiling. Covenant posture aims higher: you keep your word when it stops paying, you want the other party to do well, and you still write it all down. Here is how the Word sets that higher mark.
rto7-covenant-over-contract.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. A signed page is not the finish line because a contract only tells you what to do when someone leaves. Write it down anyway, plainly, because the record protects the weaker party. Then carry the higher posture Yahweh models in His everlasting covenant: keep the agreement when the wind changes (Psalms 15:4), and want the person across the counter to thrive. The paperwork is the floor. Faithfulness that does not depend on their usefulness is the aim.

teen.open: A signed deal is the minimum, not the goal. The goal is keeping your word and wanting the other person to do well.
teen.close: So write the deal down, and then live above it. Keep your promise even when it costs you, and care whether the other person wins too.

senior.open: A contract is written for the day someone walks away. This lesson asks us to aim higher than that: to keep our word as people of covenant, not merely as parties to a document.
senior.close: So the signed page is the floor. Document the agreement fully, and then keep it as Yahweh keeps His covenant: when it costs you, and with real concern that the other party does well.

rto8-marketing-vision-and-going-to-get-t.reason: The title promises customers-as-marketing and a business that stands; that answer (reputation built on how people were treated leaving; built by wisdom, established by understanding) sits near the end, then the lesson closes on balance and provision.
rto8-marketing-vision-and-going-to-get-t.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How do you build a business that stands, and why are your customers your marketing? Marketing is telling the truth about something worth having to people who would be better off with it. In rent-to-own, most agreements end in a return, so your name is made by how people were treated on the way out. The business stands when it is built by wisdom, established by understanding, and filled by knowledge, with vision and the power to get wealth coming from Yahweh.
rto8-marketing-vision-and-going-to-get-t.example: TWO RETURNS, TWO REPUTATIONS. Say two customers bring back a sofa in the same week. One is met with pressure and a cold counter. The other is thanked, helped with the pickup, and told the door is open next time. Neither one is buying today. But next month, one of them is telling a neighbour where to go, and the other is telling a neighbour where not to go. That conversation is your marketing department at work.
rto8-marketing-vision-and-going-to-get-t.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Your customers are your marketing because the people who left, and how they were treated, tell the neighbourhood who you are. A business that stands gets there in order: vision received from Yahweh in His Word, the power to earn that He supplies (Deuteronomy 8:18), and Uncle Russell's rule of going to get the information, the understanding and the skill. Wisdom builds the house, Understanding makes it stand, Knowledge fills the chambers (Proverbs 24:3-4). Treat people well on the way out, and the house carries its own name.

teen.open: Your best ads are the people you served, even the ones who left. A business that lasts is built on wisdom, not hype.
teen.close: So treat people right, especially on the way out. Keep learning, keep getting understanding, and let Yahweh give the vision. That is how a business stands.

senior.open: The title makes a plain claim: in a business like this, your customers are your marketing. The lesson shows why, and what makes a business stand over time.
senior.close: So the answer is settled. Your reputation is built by how people were treated, most of all as they left, and a business stands when wisdom builds it, understanding establishes it, and knowledge fills it, with Yahweh supplying the vision and the power to earn.
